title: What Does a ProcGen Generalization Gap Measure?Action Rules, Convergence, and the Missing Random Floor

paper.title: What Does a ProcGen Generalization Gap Measure? Action Rules, Convergence, and the Missing Random Floor
paper.abstract:
Abstract A generalization gap in reinforcement learning (return on training levels minus
return on held-out levels) is usually reported without a reference point. We argue
that the missing reference is a measured random floor: the return of a
uniform-random policy on the same levels under the same harness. On ProcGen, the
floor changes what several standard numbers mean. On identical checkpoints and
levels across eight environments, switching between sampled and greedy (argmax)
test-time actions moves held-out return in both directions, and greedy evaluation
takes three environments to or below the floor: in miner, the sampled policy
scores 4.9 × \times the floor on held-out levels while its argmax scores below it.
Raw policy entropy places seven of eight environments short of convergence, but
35–65% of that entropy is spread across actions with identical effects; after
merging them, one to three remain short, and against the floor only heist has
learned nothing that transfers. An audit of twelve prior ProcGen codebases finds
that all eleven with held-out evaluation sample test-time actions for their
policy-gradient agents, nine by default rather than explicit choice, and six
report running in-loop averages rather than evaluating a fixed checkpoint.
Applied to our own case study, the same checks grade down a statistically
significant encoder effect and rule out a within-encoder train-vs-test CKA
statistic. We recommend that every reported gap state its action rule, use a
matched and seeded protocol, and report the random floor on both level sets.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A generalization gap in reinforcement learning (RL)—return on training levels minus return on held-out levels—is the field’s headline transfer metric ( Cobbe et al., 2019 ; Kirk et al., 2023 ) , and it is almost always reported without a reference point. This paper argues that the missing reference is a measured random floor: the return of a uniform-random policy on the same levels, under the same harness. It costs minutes to measure, and on the benchmark we study it changes what several standard numbers mean. The setting is ProcGen ( Cobbe et al., 2020 ) , a standard benchmark for generalization in deep RL. Each ProcGen environment procedurally generates levels : episodes whose layout, textures, and object placement vary under a seeded generator. An agent is trained on a fixed set of levels (here 200) and evaluated on held-out levels it has never interacted with (here 100), drawn from the same generator. Algorithms, architectures, and regularizers are compared by their gaps, and representation-level explanations are attached to the winners. The first thing the floor exposes is that the test-time action rule decides which policy gets measured. An agent’s action can be sampled from its action distribution or chosen greedily as the most probable action (argmax). For a converged policy the two nearly coincide; for one that has not converged they are different policies, and the difference is not a scalar inflation. On identical checkpoints and identical levels, switching rules moves held-out return in both directions across eight environments (Section 5.1 ). In miner, sampling from the trained policy scores 4.9 × 4.9\times the floor on held-out levels, while its argmax—the rule our own main tables use—scores below the floor. A policy that demonstrably transfers is measured as worse than chance. The second is convergence. How much a gap says about transfer depends on whether the policy has learned a training-level behavior to transfer. A common proxy is policy entropy against the maximum of ln ⁡ 15 = 2.708 \ln 15=2.708 over ProcGen’s 15 discrete actions; by that measure a standard 8M-step budget leaves seven of eight environments at 74–95% of maximum. But ProcGen games have between 4 and 11 functionally distinct actions, and 35–65% of the measured entropy is spread across actions with identical effects (Appendix D ). Against the floor, one environment, heist, has learned nothing that transfers: its sampled held-out return sits at the floor at 8M and at or marginally below it after a threefold budget extension, while its training-level return reaches twice the floor. Entropy remains useful as a cheap screen. It agrees with the floor at the extremes and over-calls in the middle, most clearly on bossfight, which it flags as non-converged and whose policy scores clearly above a near-zero floor ( z ≈ 2.6 z\approx 2.6 – 2.7 2.7 ). High entropy is not proof that training failed, and a stochastic policy is a legitimate object of evaluation. Neither check is standard. Auditing the released evaluation code of twelve prior ProcGen codebases, we find that all eleven that evaluate on held-out levels sample the test-time actions of their policy-gradient agents. Nine do so through a default function argument ( deterministic=False ) that no call site overrides or through the training rollout’s own sampling call; two set the rule explicitly. Two codebases also evaluate value-based agents, which act greedily (Impoola’s DQN) or ϵ \epsilon -greedily (EDE’s own method). Six read test numbers from a held-out rollout running inside the training loop, averaged over episodes that span policy updates, rather than evaluating a fixed checkpoint (Section 4 ). Sampling on both level sets is a matched protocol, and by the analysis above it measures the policy that was trained; what the audit documents is a rule that in most codebases is inherited rather than set, so that its consequences for the reported gap go unexamined. We apply the same checks to our own case study (two encoder architectures, all else fixed) and to our own harness. A statistically significant encoder effect on heist turns out to compare two below-floor held-out returns; an unseeded evaluation-level draw moved a p p -value across the significance boundary; and a representation statistic we had computed, within-encoder train-vs-test CKA, proves invalid on disjoint observation sets. Our contributions: 1. A measured random floor as the reference point for generalization gaps, cheap to compute, reported for eight ProcGen environments on both level sets. 2. Evidence that the test-time action rule decides which policy is measured: on identical checkpoints and levels the two rules disagree in both directions, and greedy evaluation takes three of eight environments to or below the floor, including one whose sampled policy scores 4.9 × 4.9\times it. 3. A recalibration of entropy-based convergence checks: effective action counts per game, merged-action entropy, and a behavioral check against the floor, which together reduce seven of eight environments short of convergence to one to three, and identify the one environment whose policy has learned nothing that transfers. 4. A twelve-codebase audit of ProcGen evaluation practice, verified against pinned commits to the file and line, including a correction of our own earlier classification. 5. A self-audit: an encoder effect graded down by the floor, a level-draw variance source in our harness, and a 2 × 2 2\times 2 control with a closed-form null showing that within-encoder train-vs-test CKA is invalid on disjoint inputs.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Evaluation methodology in RL. Henderson et al. (2018) document reproducibility failures caused by underspecified evaluation procedures; Agarwal et al. (2021) argue for statistically rigorous reporting (interquartile means, stratified bootstrap intervals) given RL’s small seed counts. Those works ask whether results are reported rigorously. We ask a question one step earlier: whether the two numbers being differenced mean what they appear to, which requires knowing which policy produced them and where chance lies. Why the default exists. Prior ProcGen protocols were designed largely for ranking . The original benchmark ( Cobbe et al., 2020 ) and the NeurIPS 2020 ProcGen competition ( Mohanty et al., 2021 ) average many episodes for a stable leaderboard, a setting in which stochastic action selection is internally consistent across submissions. The default is thus a defensible design choice, and by Section 5.1 a sound one for policies that have not converged; what was lost when it was reused is the reason for it. When a single train-minus-test difference becomes a paper’s headline number, which rule produced it, whether it describes one checkpoint, and where it sits relative to chance all bear directly on what it means. Policy convergence. Beukman et al. (2026) document that PPO training frequently stagnates far short of a task-solving policy; several recent PPO variants target exactly this stagnation ( Rahman and Xue, 2022 ; Lixandru, 2024 ; Rahman, 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ) . Our increment is to show that stagnation confounds the measurement rather than just the performance. A gap computed on a stagnated policy is confounded with incomplete optimization, and is correspondingly weaker evidence about transfer. Encoders and representation diagnostics. The IMPALA CNN ( Espeholt et al., 2018 ) is the standard ProcGen encoder; feature pyramid networks ( Lin et al., 2017 ) are a multi-scale design imported from object detection, and VSOP-3D ( Jesson and Jiang, 2024 ) reports ProcGen gains from combining architectural scale-up with an algorithmic change ( Jesson et al., 2024 ) . For representation analysis we use linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) , a similarity measure between two networks’ internal representations, with the caveats of Davari et al. (2022) , and the dormant-neuron ratio ( Sokar et al., 2023 ) , the fraction of network units that have effectively stopped activating.

sections.heading: 3.1 Encoder architectures
sections.text: Two encoders, identical except for one design choice. Both share the same three-block IMPALA convolutional backbone. The baseline flattens the final feature map and projects it to a 256-dimensional representation. The multiscale FPN variant additionally fuses intermediate feature maps from all three blocks, top-down, before projecting to the same 256-dimensional space (521k vs. 622k parameters; architectural details in Appendix F ). The policy and value heads, the RL algorithm, and every hyperparameter are identical across the two conditions, so any downstream difference is attributable to the encoder.

sections.heading: 3.2 Training setup
sections.text: We train agents with PPO, a standard on-policy deep RL algorithm: the agent alternates between collecting experience with its current policy (a rollout ) and updating the policy on that experience. The 8M runs use 16 parallel environment copies, and the 25M runs and the heist entropy-coefficient retrains use 256 (the CleanRL ProcGen default is 64); all use 200 training levels and an otherwise standard configuration (Appendix F ); each condition (encoder × \times environment) is repeated with 3 random seeds—independent training runs differing only in random initialization. At 25M, starpilot and heist use 9 and 6 seeds per encoder; the additional seeds were trained later with an identical configuration. The baseline budget is 8M environment steps across eight environments; a budget extension trains three environments to 25M steps.

sections.heading: 3.3 Evaluation protocol
sections.text: Three properties of an evaluation protocol determine what a reported gap measures. Which policy. At evaluation time an action can be sampled from the policy’s action distribution or chosen greedily as the highest-probability action (argmax). Sampling evaluates the policy that was trained. Argmax evaluates a deterministic policy derived from it, which coincides with the trained policy only when the action distribution is sharply peaked. A harness can describe itself as deterministic while sampling at every step, so the rule has to be checked in code, not read from a configuration name. Which checkpoint. A commonly logged metric is the running mean return of recent episodes collected during training. Such a number averages over several policy versions and describes no single checkpoint, and comparing it against a separately measured return would also conflate a difference in procedure with the train/test shift. Relative to what. A return is interpretable only against a reference. We measure a uniform-random floor on both level sets with the same harness, level draws, and episode accounting as the trained policies (Appendix D ). Cobbe et al. (2020) normalize ProcGen returns with fixed per-game constants. The floor used here differs in being measured rather than fixed: it is taken under the evaluating harness, level draws and episode accounting, on both level sets, so it moves with the protocol it calibrates. Our main tables evaluate both level sets identically with greedy argmax, 128 episodes per measurement at the 25M budget and 64 at 8M, at the final checkpoint, with an episode burn-in and complete rollout windows. Section 5.1 re-evaluates every 8M checkpoint under both rules on seeded level draws, against the floor. Given what that section finds, greedy numbers for environments short of convergence describe the argmax policy, and we read them that way.

sections.heading: 3.4 Convergence checks
sections.text: How much a generalization gap says about transfer depends on whether the policy has learned a training-level behavior in the first place. A gap measured on a policy that has not is confounded with incomplete optimization: harder to read as transfer, not uninterpretable. We use two checks. The behavioral check compares held-out and training-level return, under the policy’s own sampled actions, with the random floor; it needs no threshold, normalizer, or action-space assumption. The screen is final-checkpoint policy entropy relative to the maximum-entropy uniform policy ( ln ⁡ 15 = 2.708 \ln 15=2.708 ), in three tiers: converged (entropy < 2.0 <2.0 ), partial ( [ 2.0 , 2.3 ] [2.0,2.3] ), non-converged ( > 2.3 >2.3 ). The screen is cheap and routinely logged; the behavioral check is what a tier should be read against. Entropy alone cannot deliver a verdict: a high-entropy policy may be a legitimately stochastic policy and a legitimate object of evaluation, and a low-entropy policy may still perform poorly. Entropy is the mean over the train- and test-level evaluation passes; at 25M we report heist under both that convention and the test-level value alone, because the two differ enough to change its label (Appendix B ). The entropy bonus is not the only configuration choice that moves the measurement. Retraining heist with c H = 0.001 c_{H}=0.001 instead of the default 0.01 0.01 gives a terminal entropy of 2.113 ± 0.038 2.113\pm 0.038 ( 78.0 % 78.0\% of maximum; n = 3 n{=}3 seeds per encoder, 8M), against 2.565 2.565 ( 94.7 % 94.7\% ) for the default runs. Those retrains, however, used 256 parallel environments rather than the 16 of the default 8M runs (Appendix F ), so the difference cannot be attributed to c H c_{H} ; it shows only that the screen’s value depends on the training configuration, which is one more reason to read it against the behavioral check. The two checks agree at the extremes and disagree in the middle (Table 3 ). Starpilot is converged by entropy and far above the floor; heist is the least converged by entropy and the only environment whose sampled held-out return is at the floor. Between them the screen over-calls. Bossfight is non-converged by entropy yet its sampled policy scores clearly above the floor on held-out levels ( 1.38 1.38 vs. 0.09 0.09 , z ≈ 2.6 z\approx 2.6 ), and dodgeball, also non-converged, is above its floor ( 1.12 1.12 vs. 0.47 0.47 , z ≈ 3.0 z\approx 3.0 ). Part of the over-call is the action space: entropy over ProcGen’s 15 raw actions counts probability spread across actions with identical effects as indecision, and 35–65% of each environment’s raw entropy is of that kind (Appendix D ). Merging equivalent actions before computing entropy leaves one environment short of the converged band (heist) when equivalence is determined state by state, and three (dodgeball, bossfight, heist) under a single partition per game; these counts depend on expressing the 2.0 and 2.3 cuts as fractions of the maximum, which is our choice. We keep raw-action entropy for the tiers because it is what practitioners log, and read a partial or non-converged tier as a prompt to run the behavioral check, not as a finding that the policy has not learned. Two robustness checks address whether the entropy cut point is load-bearing. First, sweeping the converged/partial boundary across [ 1.8 , 2.2 ] [1.8,2.2] leaves the two extreme calls unchanged (starpilot is converged and heist non-converged at every value), while the intermediate environments near 2.0 move with the cut point, which is precisely why they carry the partial label rather than a verdict (Appendix B ). This sweep bounds the borderline calls only: starpilot ( 1.799 1.799 ) and heist ( 2.565 2.565 ) are the extremes of the observed range, so no interior cut point could reclassify them, and their stability under the sweep follows from the data layout rather than from robustness. Second, a diagnostic that never thresholds the final entropy (the total collapse of entropy from its initial plateau, combined with training-set return) ranks environments consistently with the tiers (Spearman ρ = 0.79 \rho=0.79 ; Appendix C ); it shares the terminal-entropy trajectory as an input, so it is a second reading rather than a fully independent one.

sections.heading: 3.5 Statistical analysis
sections.text: Encoder and train-vs-test comparisons use Welch’s t t -test. Where we pool across independent draws (seeds), per-draw two-sided p p -values are combined with Fisher’s method, with Stouffer’s Z Z on the one-sided p p -values as a directional cross-check; confidence intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap ( 10 4 10^{4} resamples). Per-environment pooled results, and one instructive case where the omnibus and directional combiners disagree, are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 4 Field-Wide Audit
sections.text: To document how ProcGen generalization numbers are produced in practice, we audited the released evaluation code of twelve prior ProcGen codebases spanning ICML, NeurIPS, RLC, and arXiv from 2019 to 2025. What we looked for. For each repository we located the code path that produces the paper’s reported test numbers. We then classified two binary properties: (i) stochastic evaluation , whether test-time actions are sampled from the policy distribution rather than chosen by greedy argmax; and (ii) in-loop test returns , whether reported test returns are read from a held-out rollout that runs concurrently inside the training loop—stepped alongside training, never reset between updates, and reported as a running mean over the most recent completed episodes, which therefore span several policy versions—rather than from a dedicated evaluation of a fixed checkpoint. Property (ii) is deliberately narrower than it may sound: in every codebase we mark, the held-out environments or workers contribute no gradient, so the test returns are not returns from the rollout the policy is trained on. Classifications were made against a pinned commit, and the evidencing file and line for every entry are listed in Appendix E so the classification is reproducible against the precise code state. For codebases with an explicit evaluation script, the cited line is the test-time action-selection call; for the in-loop codebases, the cited lines are where the held-out environment or worker is created and where its running return is reported. What we found. Eleven of twelve codebases perform held-out evaluation; all eleven evaluate their policy-gradient agents stochastically, and six of those additionally report in-loop test returns (Table 1 ). UCB-DrAC ( Raileanu et al., 2021 ) is the most explicit instance, passing deterministic=False at test.py line 42. Impoola ( Trumpp et al., 2025 ) also sets the rule explicitly, through a documented configuration option: its PPO evaluation samples and its DQN evaluation is greedy, as its paper states. EDE ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) is itself a value-based method: its released code samples when evaluating its PPO baseline, which is the row we classify, while EDE’s own agent is evaluated ϵ \epsilon -greedily with ϵ = 0.05 \epsilon=0.05 , the standard DQN evaluation protocol. For a value-based agent the greedy action is the trained policy, so neither case bears on the sampled-versus-argmax analysis of Section 5.1 , which concerns stochastic policies. VSOP and VSOP-3D ( Jesson et al., 2024 ; Jesson and Jiang, 2024 ) step a separate held-out environment once per training step and report the mean of its last 100 episodes. A classification we checked and rejected. These six codebases are easily read as rollout-mode —reading test returns off the on-policy training rollout, a train-vs-test procedure mismatch—and our own first pass classified them that way. Checking each against its pinned commit shows that classification is wrong. In mixreg, the ProcGen baseline, and IBAC-SNI the test numbers come from a dedicated MPI test worker whose gradient is weighted to zero; in RAD, VSOP, and VSOP-3D they come from a separate held-out environment whose transitions are discarded. In all six the train number comes from the matching in-loop procedure on the training levels, so train and test are measured the same way. What remains is the weaker property defined above: the test number is a sampled-action running average taken during training, not a measurement of the final policy. Our cited location for mixreg was also wrong: it pointed at an evaluation runner the training script never enables. The twelfth, PPG ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , trains on the full level distribution and performs no held-out evaluation in its released code, so neither classification applies (n/a). Provenance. Nine of the eleven set no rule at the point of evaluation. Three (DAAC, PLR, and EDE’s PPO baseline) inherit sampling through a default argument that no call site overrides, and the six in-loop codebases sample through the training rollout’s own sampling call, which has no deterministic path. In these nine, nothing in the evaluation code selects the rule or states a reason for it. That is how the practice became field-wide: an evaluation default propagated through copied harness code. The two exceptions show that the rule can be set deliberately: UCB-DrAC passes deterministic=False at the call site, and Impoola exposes the rule as a configuration option, sampling for PPO and acting greedily for DQN. By the analysis of Section 5.1 , the default happens to be the better of the two rules for policies that have not converged; the concern is that where it is inherited, its consequences for the reported gap go unexamined. Scope of the claim. We audited released evaluation code, not results as reported in papers, and we do not claim any specific published number is wrong. The claim is about what the procedure can support. A gap whose train and test numbers come from different procedures cannot distinguish a protocol difference from a distributional one; we found no such case in the audit, but the hazard is general. An in-loop gap is matched, but it averages over the policies visited during training rather than measuring any one of them. sections.heading: 5.1 The action rule decides which policy is measured
sections.text: Table 2 evaluates the same 48 checkpoints (8M steps; eight environments × \times two encoders × \times three seeds) on the same held-out levels under both rules, 128 episodes per run, alongside a uniform-random policy on identical level draws. None of what follows is a scalar inflation. One checkpoint, two answers. Miner shows the whole effect in one pair of numbers. Sampling from the trained 8M policies scores 5.69 ± 0.33 5.69\pm 0.33 on held-out levels, 4.9 × 4.9\times the random floor of 1.17 ± 0.11 1.17\pm 0.11 ; the argmax of the same weights scores 0.64 ± 0.10 0.64\pm 0.10 , below the floor in all six runs. The policy has learned something that transfers, and greedy evaluation—the rule our own main tables use—reports it as worse than chance. Coinrun shows the same pattern more weakly: sampled 5.82 5.82 , above its floor of 3.28 3.28 ; greedy 3.55 3.55 , indistinguishable from it. The rule’s effect has no fixed sign. Sampled return exceeds greedy return in miner, coinrun and heist ( 3.05 3.05 vs. 0.51 0.51 ). Greedy exceeds sampled in bossfight ( 2.42 2.42 vs. 1.38 1.38 , all six runs) and fruitbot ( 25.63 25.63 vs. 22.74 22.74 ). The remaining three are within noise, among them starpilot, the one environment converged by entropy ( 17.97 17.97 vs. 18.36 18.36 ). There is no single correction factor that converts one rule’s numbers into the other’s. Why argmax can fall below chance. Argmax of a policy that has not converged is a different policy. It commits every state to whichever action narrowly leads, and where that preference is arbitrary the committed behavior can be worse than choosing at random—for example, repeating one failing trajectory where random play would eventually stumble onto the goal (a plausible mechanism, not one we isolate). A second candidate, specific to ProcGen’s action space, is that argmax over raw actions can choose against the policy’s own preference when the probability of one behavior is split across functionally equivalent actions (Appendix D ); in miner, where the three leftward and three rightward moves each collapse to one, this can happen at any step. We do not test it here. When the sampled number is at chance, it is accurate. Heist is the other case. Its sampled held-out return ( 3.05 ± 0.22 3.05\pm 0.22 ) is indistinguishable from the floor ( 3.15 ± 0.07 3.15\pm 0.07 ). Heist pays 0 0 or 10 10 per level, so the sampled policy completes about 30 % 30\% of held-out levels, random play about 31 % 31\% , and the greedy policy about 5 % 5\% . Unlike miner’s, heist’s sampled number accurately reports a policy that transfers nothing beyond random play. Read as a ratio, sampled over greedy— 8.3 × 8.3\times for IMPALA ( 2.58 2.58 vs. 0.31 0.31 ) and 5.0 × 5.0\times for FPN ( 3.52 3.52 vs. 0.70 0.70 )—it looks like stochastic inflation; read against the floor, it is greedy deflation below chance. What this does to the gap. Applying one rule to both level sets is a matched measurement, and our audit found no codebase that takes train and test numbers from structurally different procedures (Section 4 ). The concern is not a mismatch. It is that the rule decides which policy is measured, and for a policy that has not converged the two candidates differ in kind, so the gaps differ too. At 8M the sampled gap exceeds the greedy gap in heist ( 1.46 1.46 vs. 0.76 0.76 ) and miner ( 1.60 1.60 vs. 0.55 0.55 ), and is similar or smaller elsewhere. At 25M on heist ( n = 6 n{=}6 seeds per encoder; Table 15 ) the sampled gap is 1.69 × 1.69\times the greedy one ( 4.36 ± 0.19 4.36\pm 0.19 vs. 2.58 ± 0.26 2.58\pm 0.26 ; Welch t = 5.47 t{=}5.47 , p = 2.4 × 10 − 5 p{=}2.4\times 10^{-5} ), and the floor says what each gap is made of. Under sampling, training-level return is twice the floor ( 7.17 7.17 vs. 3.54 3.54 ) and held-out return is at or marginally below it ( 2.81 ± 0.16 2.81\pm 0.16 vs. 3.15 ± 0.07 3.15\pm 0.07 , z = − 1.95 z=-1.95 ): a policy that has learned its training levels and transfers nothing. Under greedy selection, training-level return is at the floor ( 3.38 3.38 ) and held-out return is below it ( 0.79 0.79 ): a difference between chance and sub-chance. Neither gap is interpretable without the floor, and the sampled one is the more faithful description of the policy that was trained. sections.heading: 5.2 Convergence across eight environments
sections.text: Table 3 sets the entropy screen beside the behavioral check at 8M. By raw entropy only starpilot converges ( 1.799 1.799 , 66.4% of maximum); four environments are partial, and dodgeball (89.5%), bossfight (87.9%), and heist (94.7%) are non-converged. Against the floor, seven of eight sampled policies are above chance on held-out levels, and only heist is at it. Merging functionally equivalent actions moves the screen toward the behavioral reading: state by state, only heist remains short of the converged band. Bossfight is the sharpest disagreement. The screen calls it non-converged; its sampled and greedy policies both sit above the near-zero floor on held-out levels ( z ≈ 2.6 z\approx 2.6 and 2.7 2.7 ). We report this as a misclassification by the screen. A raw-entropy tier says that the policy’s distribution over raw actions is broad, and for bossfight that breadth sits on top of a policy that has plainly learned; it does not say that the policy has failed to learn. sections.heading: 5.3 Budget extension to 25M steps
sections.text: Is non-convergence just insufficient training? We extend starpilot, fruitbot, and heist to 25M steps (Figure 1 ). These runs also use 256 parallel environments rather than 16 (Section 7 ), so the extension changes batch size and the number of policy updates along with the step budget. Starpilot’s entropy crosses the threshold at roughly 5–7M steps and continues to 55–63% of maximum. Fruitbot’s raw training-log entropy sits at 80–82% of maximum across the 17M additional steps and plateaus (against 78.3% at 8M, an evaluation-pass value on a different convention). But at 8M, 65% of fruitbot’s raw entropy is spread over equivalent actions and its policy is far above the floor at 8M, so the plateau is a limit of the screen, not evidence that fruitbot failed to learn. Heist is the informative case. Its entropy declines modestly (train-level 77–83%, test-level 86–87%). Behaviorally, three times the budget lifts its sampled training-level return to twice the floor ( 7.17 7.17 vs. 3.54 3.54 ; Table 15 ) while its sampled held-out return stays at or marginally below the floor ( 2.81 ± 0.16 2.81\pm 0.16 vs. 3.15 ± 0.07 3.15\pm 0.07 , z = − 1.95 z=-1.95 ; the floor is measured on the same level sets but a different level draw). The additional environment steps raised training-level return, and none of that improvement transfers. Training length cannot stand in for a convergence check, and for heist the check that matters is behavioral. Convergence does not, however, make the gap stable. Starpilot is the one environment converged by the screen, and its gap changes sign between budgets: − 0.99 -0.99 [ − 1.66 , − 0.35 ] [-1.66,-0.35] at 8M against + 3.11 +3.11 [ 1.27 , 4.81 ] [1.27,4.81] at 25M (Table 5 ), scoring held-out levels slightly above training levels early and clearly below them later. Convergence makes a gap easier to read; it does not make the reading budget-independent. The two budgets also differ in parallelism, so the sign change cannot be attributed to budget alone. sections.heading: 5.4 A third variance source, in our own harness
sections.text: The matched-protocol requirement extends to a place we did not initially look: the random draw of the evaluation level set itself. ProcGen samples the evaluated subset of held-out levels without a fixed seed, so re-evaluating identical checkpoints under an otherwise identical protocol instantiates a different level subset each run. On heist this moves the encoder test-return p p -value from 0.04 0.04 to 0.13 0.13 across draws, crossing the conventional significance boundary, while the gap difference survives both draws ( p = 0.004 p=0.004 – 0.011 0.011 ). We report the range rather than a combined p p -value across draws: Fisher’s method assumes independence, and re-evaluations of the same checkpoints share the trained weights, so pooling over them would be anticonservative (pooling across seeds, which have disjoint RNG streams, is unaffected). We therefore seed the evaluation draw and report the gap as robust but the test-return difference as not; a third, seeded draw of the same checkpoints agrees (gap p = 0.0023 p=0.0023 , test return p = 0.12 p=0.12 ). We flag this deliberately. It is the same class of unexamined protocol variance we audit in others, it was in our own harness, and it changed a conclusion. An evaluation protocol is not fully specified until every random draw in it is either fixed or marginalized over.

sections.heading: 5.5 Encoder comparison, convergence-conditional
sections.text: The case study asks whether a multi-scale encoder generalizes better than the standard one. How far the answer can be read as a statement about generalization depends on convergence and on where the returns sit relative to the floor (Table 4 ). At convergence: null. On starpilot at 25M ( n = 9 n{=}9 seeds), test return ( p = 0.728 p{=}0.728 ) and gap ( p = 0.481 p{=}0.481 ) are both null. The capacity diagnostic agrees: dormant-neuron ratios overlap at every threshold (full tables in Appendix F ). Outside convergence: an apparent effect, graded down. On heist at 25M ( n = 6 n{=}6 ), FPN’s gap is significantly smaller ( 2.11 ± 0.21 2.11\pm 0.21 vs. 3.40 ± 0.27 3.40\pm 0.27 ; p = 0.004 p=0.004 – 0.011 0.011 across the two unseeded evaluation draws, and p = 0.0023 p=0.0023 on a seeded third draw). The floor says what those numbers are. They are greedy returns: both encoders’ held-out returns ( 0.47 0.47 and 0.89 0.89 ) sit far below the held-out floor of 3.15 3.15 , and their training-level returns ( 3.87 3.87 and 2.99 2.99 ) straddle the training floor of 3.54 3.54 . The encoder difference compares two below-chance measurements of argmax policies, and the sampled policy they stand in for transfers nothing beyond random play (Section 5.3 ). It is real as a measurement and weak evidence about generalization. Decomposing it shows why caution is warranted even at face value. Of the 1.29 1.29 -point gap difference, 0.87 0.87 (68%) comes from lower FPN train return rather than better transfer, and the test-return difference is not robust across evaluation draws ( p p ranges across the boundary, 0.04 0.04 – 0.13 0.13 ). Cross-encoder CKA is markedly highest in the converged environment ( 0.757 / 0.783 0.757/0.783 train/test, against 0.518 0.518 – 0.678 0.678 elsewhere), consistent with convergence driving distinct architectures toward a shared solution, though tier is confounded with environment identity across three environments, so we claim only the converged-vs-rest contrast. A representation diagnostic that does not work. Within-encoder train-vs-test CKA is a natural way to ask how level-specific a representation is: compute each encoder’s representation of train-level and of held-out-level observations and compare the two. It does not work. Linear CKA compares two representation matrices row by row, so row i i of each must be the same input, and no valid correspondence exists between two disjoint observation sets; here 1024 train-level observations are set against 1024 different test-level ones. The value is not noise—it sits 8 to 97 standard deviations above its row-permutation null (per-seed range, starpilot and fruitbot at 8M)—but a 2 × 2 2\times 2 control identifies what it responds to: holding the row alignment while removing the domain shift entirely (train-vs-train) returns the same value as the train-vs-test comparison, and wherever the representation has appreciable effective rank, shuffling one side’s rows collapses both, by 4.6 4.6 – 7.2 × 7.2\times on fruitbot at 8M. It reads the episode-timestep alignment shared by the two observation batches, not the level set, and its permutation null is exactly PR X ​ PR Y / ( n − 1 ) \sqrt{\mathrm{PR}_{X}\mathrm{PR}_{Y}}/(n{-}1) in the two participation ratios, so the between-encoder offset tracks effective rank. Read naively, the statistic says FPN is 3.44 × 3.44\times less train-specific than IMPALA on fruitbot at 8M; in units of each side’s own null the ratio is 1.14 × 1.14\times , and seed by seed it straddles one (Appendix G ). The cross-encoder rows are unaffected: they compare two encoders on identical observations, which is correctly paired. We report the diagnostic and its failure, rather than omitting it, because the failure generalizes beyond ProcGen: any train-vs-test representation comparison computed with a row-paired similarity measure on disjoint inputs is exposed to it. sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: Report the rule and the floor. The recommendation that follows from Section 5.1 is not “use sampling”; it is to state the action rule and report a measured random floor on both level sets. What distinguishes the two rules is which policy they evaluate: sampling evaluates the policy that was trained, argmax a deterministic policy derived from it. The two coincide at convergence—starpilot’s rules agree within noise ( 17.97 17.97 vs. 18.36 18.36 )—so argmax is safe there, and unsafe exactly where policies have not converged: every floor crossing in Table 2 occurs in an environment the entropy screen flags as partial or non-converged. Argmax remains reasonable when the deterministic policy is itself the object of interest, or as a second number beside the sampled one; its danger is being read as the trained policy’s competence. Sampling is not self-interpreting either: heist’s sampled numbers are accurate, and only the floor shows that they are accurate reports of chance. What a trustworthy gap requires. Stated as a procedure: evaluate a fixed checkpoint rather than a running in-loop average; state the action rule and apply it identically to both level sets; seed (or marginalize over) every random draw in the evaluation pipeline, including the level-subset draw; measure the random floor on both level sets with the same harness; and check convergence behaviorally, against that floor, using entropy as a screen. Each step is cheap, and the floor costs minutes; none is standard. Where it matters most. The rules diverge, and returns sit nearest the floor, in environments the entropy screen flags, which are also where apparent gaps look largest and most interesting. A gap there needs its floor more than anywhere else. Reliability, stated precisely. This is the paper’s standing position on convergence. Our claim concerns whether a number supports the inference drawn from it, not that all such numbers are noise, and not that a high-entropy policy is illegitimate: a stochastic policy is a real policy and can be a proper object of evaluation. What convergence governs is whether the train-minus-test gap supports an inference about transfer. An environment whose held-out return sits well above the random floor (fruitbot, 25.4 25.4 greedy mean across six runs at 8M, against − 2.66 -2.66 for uniform-random play) retains transferable behavior, and its gap is cautiously interpretable whatever its entropy tier; a policy at the floor (heist, sampled 3.05 3.05 against 3.15 3.15 ) supports much less. The checks grade interpretability; they do not zero it out.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: Seed counts. Most conditions use n = 3 n{=}3 seeds ( n = 6 n{=}6 heist, n = 9 n{=}9 starpilot at 25M), so the encoder comparison has limited statistical power. The two claim classes differ here. The action-rule and convergence findings rest on effects that do not turn on seed count: floor crossings in all six runs of heist and miner, a 4.9 × 4.9\times sampled-to-floor margin on miner, and a twelve-codebase audit. The encoder comparison does turn on seed count, and we present it as a case study rather than a finding. The floor is one reference. A uniform-random policy is the simplest reference and calibrates only the lower end; a stronger reference, such as a scripted policy or one trained to convergence, would calibrate the upper end, and we do not report one. The floor’s level draws match the 8M re-evaluation exactly but not the 25M heist comparison, which used a different seeded draw from the same level sets. Random-weight guessing ( Oller et al., 2020 ) , which evaluates untrained networks rather than uniform actions, would give a structured lower reference that we have not measured. Our own tables use argmax. Tables 13 and 4 and the gaps in Table 3 were measured with greedy selection before the analysis of Section 5.1 . For environments short of convergence they describe the argmax policy; apart from heist (Table 15 ) we have not re-run the 25M budget under sampling. One threshold, one suite, one algorithm. The entropy screen uses a single threshold, swept but not derived, on one benchmark suite with one RL algorithm (PPO), over raw rather than functionally distinct actions. The suite is eight of ProcGen’s sixteen games, in the easy distribution mode only. The action-equivalence classes are measured from the rendered observation over a five-step horizon, and could miss effects that surface later. Success-rate stability over training would be a natural further check and requires per-step return logs we did not export. Parallel environments. The 8M runs use 16 parallel environments and the 25M runs 256, against the CleanRL default of 64. Each PPO update therefore sees a smaller batch at 8M and a larger one at 25M, and with 256-step rollouts the 25M runs make about 381 policy updates against about 1953 at 8M. The budget extension is thus an extension in environment steps rather than optimization steps, and it changes batch size along with budget. Beukman et al. (2026) show that PPO stagnation can be relieved by scaling the number of parallel environments; our 25M runs used four times the default and heist and fruitbot still did not converge, but the 8M entropy levels may partly reflect the smaller batch. The action-rule and floor findings describe the checkpoints as trained and do not depend on why a policy has not converged; the convergence counts and the 8M-to-25M comparisons do. Audit scope. The audit covers released evaluation code at pinned commits, not results as reported in papers; papers may have used unreleased evaluation scripts. Figures. The 8M entropy values are tabulated (Table 3 ) rather than plotted, because per-step traces for those runs were never exported; Figure 1 comes from per-iteration training logs. Every figure and tabulated number here is measured.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: A generalization gap is a measurement, and without a reference point it is hard to say what it measures. In ProcGen, a measured random floor shows that the test-time action rule decides which policy gets measured—a policy that transfers at 4.9 × 4.9\times chance can be scored below chance by its own argmax—and that an entropy screen over-calls non-convergence: by the behavioral check, one environment of eight has a policy that has learned nothing that transfers. The field’s policy-gradient evaluation code samples actions, in nine of eleven codebases by default rather than explicit setting, and in half the audited codebases reports running in-loop averages. We recommend three cheap additions to every reported gap: state the action rule, match and seed the protocol, and report the random floor on both level sets. Applied to our own study, they graded down our one significant result and ruled out a natural representation statistic.

Action Rules, Convergence, and the Missing Random Floor Abhisek Keshari Affiliation: Independent researcher Email: abhisek.keshari12@gmail.com Abstract A generalization gap in reinforcement learning (return on training levels minus return on held-out levels) is usually reported without a reference point. We argue that the missing reference is a measured random floor: the return of a uniform-random policy on the same levels under the same harness. On ProcGen, the floor changes what several standard numbers mean. On identical checkpoints and levels across eight environments, switching between sampled and greedy (argmax) test-time actions moves held-out return in both directions, and greedy evaluation takes three environments to or below the floor: in miner, the sampled policy scores 4.9 × \times the floor on held-out levels while its argmax scores below it. Raw policy entropy places seven of eight environments short of convergence, but 35–65% of that entropy is spread across actions with identical effects; after merging them, one to three remain short, and against the floor only heist has learned nothing that transfers. An audit of twelve prior ProcGen codebases finds that all eleven with held-out evaluation sample test-time actions for their policy-gradient agents, nine by default rather than explicit choice, and six report running in-loop averages rather than evaluating a fixed checkpoint. Applied to our own case study, the same checks grade down a statistically significant encoder effect and rule out a within-encoder train-vs-test CKA statistic. We recommend that every reported gap state its action rule, use a matched and seeded protocol, and report the random floor on both level sets. 1 Introduction A generalization gap in reinforcement learning (RL)—return on training levels minus return on held-out levels—is the field’s headline transfer metric ( Cobbe et al., 2019 ; Kirk et al., 2023 ) , and it is almost always reported without a reference point. This paper argues that the missing reference is a measured random floor: the return of a uniform-random policy on the same levels, under the same harness. It costs minutes to measure, and on the benchmark we study it changes what several standard numbers mean. The setting is ProcGen ( Cobbe et al., 2020 ) , a standard benchmark for generalization in deep RL. Each ProcGen environment procedurally generates levels : episodes whose layout, textures, and object placement vary under a seeded generator. An agent is trained on a fixed set of levels (here 200) and evaluated on held-out levels it has never interacted with (here 100), drawn from the same generator. Algorithms, architectures, and regularizers are compared by their gaps, and representation-level explanations are attached to the winners. The first thing the floor exposes is that the test-time action rule decides which policy gets measured. An agent’s action can be sampled from its action distribution or chosen greedily as the most probable action (argmax). For a converged policy the two nearly coincide; for one that has not converged they are different policies, and the difference is not a scalar inflation. On identical checkpoints and identical levels, switching rules moves held-out return in both directions across eight environments (Section 5.1 ). In miner, sampling from the trained policy scores 4.9 × 4.9\times the floor on held-out levels, while its argmax—the rule our own main tables use—scores below the floor. A policy that demonstrably transfers is measured as worse than chance. The second is convergence. How much a gap says about transfer depends on whether the policy has learned a training-level behavior to transfer. A common proxy is policy entropy against the maximum of ln ⁡ 15 = 2.708 \ln 15=2.708 over ProcGen’s 15 discrete actions; by that measure a standard 8M-step budget leaves seven of eight environments at 74–95% of maximum. But ProcGen games have between 4 and 11 functionally distinct actions, and 35–65% of the measured entropy is spread across actions with identical effects (Appendix D ). Against the floor, one environment, heist, has learned nothing that transfers: its sampled held-out return sits at the floor at 8M and at or marginally below it after a threefold budget extension, while its training-level return reaches twice the floor. Entropy remains useful as a cheap screen. It agrees with the floor at the extremes and over-calls in the middle, most clearly on bossfight, which it flags as non-converged and whose policy scores clearly above a near-zero floor ( z ≈ 2.6 z\approx 2.6 – 2.7 2.7 ). High entropy is not proof that training failed, and a stochastic policy is a legitimate object of evaluation. Neither check is standard. Auditing the released evaluation code of twelve prior ProcGen codebases, we find that all eleven that evaluate on held-out levels sample the test-time actions of their policy-gradient agents. Nine do so through a default function argument ( deterministic=False ) that no call site overrides or through the training rollout’s own sampling call; two set the rule explicitly. Two codebases also evaluate value-based agents, which act greedily (Impoola’s DQN) or ϵ \epsilon -greedily (EDE’s own method). Six read test numbers from a held-out rollout running inside the training loop, averaged over episodes that span policy updates, rather than evaluating a fixed checkpoint (Section 4 ). Sampling on both level sets is a matched protocol, and by the analysis above it measures the policy that was trained; what the audit documents is a rule that in most codebases is inherited rather than set, so that its consequences for the reported gap go unexamined. We apply the same checks to our own case study (two encoder architectures, all else fixed) and to our own harness. A statistically significant encoder effect on heist turns out to compare two below-floor held-out returns; an unseeded evaluation-level draw moved a p p -value across the significance boundary; and a representation statistic we had computed, within-encoder train-vs-test CKA, proves invalid on disjoint observation sets. Our contributions: 1. A measured random floor as the reference point for generalization gaps, cheap to compute, reported for eight ProcGen environments on both level sets. 2. Evidence that the test-time action rule decides which policy is measured: on identical checkpoints and levels the two rules disagree in both directions, and greedy evaluation takes three of eight environments to or below the floor, including one whose sampled policy scores 4.9 × 4.9\times it. 3. A recalibration of entropy-based convergence checks: effective action counts per game, merged-action entropy, and a behavioral check against the floor, which together reduce seven of eight environments short of convergence to one to three, and identify the one environment whose policy has learned nothing that transfers. 4. A twelve-codebase audit of ProcGen evaluation practice, verified against pinned commits to the file and line, including a correction of our own earlier classification. 5. Henderson et al. (2018) document reproducibility failures caused by underspecified evaluation procedures; Agarwal et al. (2021) argue for statistically rigorous reporting (interquartile means, stratified bootstrap intervals) given RL’s small seed counts. Those works ask whether results are reported rigorously. We ask a question one step earlier: whether the two numbers being differenced mean what they appear to, which requires knowing which policy produced them and where chance lies. Why the default exists. Prior ProcGen protocols were designed largely for ranking . The original benchmark ( Cobbe et al., 2020 ) and the NeurIPS 2020 ProcGen competition ( Mohanty et al., 2021 ) average many episodes for a stable leaderboard, a setting in which stochastic action selection is internally consistent across submissions. The default is thus a defensible design choice, and by Section 5.1 a sound one for policies that have not converged; what was lost when it was reused is the reason for it. When a single train-minus-test difference becomes a paper’s headline number, which rule produced it, whether it describes one checkpoint, and where it sits relative to chance all bear directly on what it means. Policy convergence. Beukman et al. (2026) document that PPO training frequently stagnates far short of a task-solving policy; several recent PPO variants target exactly this stagnation ( Rahman and Xue, 2022 ; Lixandru, 2024 ; Rahman, 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ) . Our increment is to show that stagnation confounds the measurement rather than just the performance. A gap computed on a stagnated policy is confounded with incomplete optimization, and is correspondingly weaker evidence about transfer. Encoders and representation diagnostics. The IMPALA CNN ( Espeholt et al., 2018 ) is the standard ProcGen encoder; feature pyramid networks ( Lin et al., 2017 ) are a multi-scale design imported from object detection, and VSOP-3D ( Jesson and Jiang, 2024 ) reports ProcGen gains from combining architectural scale-up with an algorithmic change ( Jesson et al., 2024 ) . For representation analysis we use linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) , a similarity measure between two networks’ internal representations, with the caveats of Davari et al. (2022) , and the dormant-neuron ratio ( Sokar et al., 2023 ) , the fraction of network units that have effectively stopped activating. 3 Method 3.1 Encoder architectures Two encoders, identical except for one design choice. Both share the same three-block IMPALA convolutional backbone. The baseline flattens the final feature map and projects it to a 256-dimensional representation. The multiscale FPN variant additionally fuses intermediate feature maps from all three blocks, top-down, before projecting to the same 256-dimensional space (521k vs. 622k parameters; architectural details in Appendix F ). The policy and value heads, the RL algorithm, and every hyperparameter are identical across the two conditions, so any downstream difference is attributable to the encoder. 3.2 Training setup We train agents with PPO, a standard on-policy deep RL algorithm: the agent alternates between collecting experience with its current policy (a rollout ) and updating the policy on that experience. The 8M runs use 16 parallel environment copies, and the 25M runs and the heist entropy-coefficient retrains use 256 (the CleanRL ProcGen default is 64); all use 200 training levels and an otherwise standard configuration (Appendix F ); each condition (encoder × \times environment) is repeated with 3 random seeds—independent training runs differing only in random initialization. At 25M, starpilot and heist use 9 and 6 seeds per encoder; the additional seeds were trained later with an identical configuration. The baseline budget is 8M environment steps across eight environments; a budget extension trains three environments to 25M steps. 3.3 Evaluation protocol Three properties of an evaluation protocol determine what a reported gap measures. Which policy. At evaluation time an action can be sampled from the policy’s action distribution or chosen greedily as the highest-probability action (argmax). Sampling evaluates the policy that was trained. Argmax evaluates a deterministic policy derived from it, which coincides with the trained policy only when the action distribution is sharply peaked. A harness can describe itself as deterministic while sampling at every step, so the rule has to be checked in code, not read from a configuration name. Which checkpoint. A commonly logged metric is the running mean return of recent episodes collected during training. Such a number averages over several policy versions and describes no single checkpoint, and comparing it against a separately measured return would also conflate a difference in procedure with the train/test shift. Relative to what. A return is interpretable only against a reference. We measure a uniform-random floor on both level sets with the same harness, level draws, and episode accounting as the trained policies (Appendix D ). Cobbe et al. (2020) normalize ProcGen returns with fixed per-game constants. The floor used here differs in being measured rather than fixed: it is taken under the evaluating harness, level draws and episode accounting, on both level sets, so it moves with the protocol it calibrates. Our main tables evaluate both level sets identically with greedy argmax, 128 episodes per measurement at the 25M budget and 64 at 8M, at the final checkpoint, with an episode burn-in and complete rollout windows. Section 5.1 re-evaluates every 8M checkpoint under both rules on seeded level draws, against the floor. Given what that section finds, greedy numbers for environments short of convergence describe the argmax policy, and we read them that way. 3.4 Convergence checks How much a generalization gap says about transfer depends on whether the policy has learned a training-level behavior in the first place. A gap measured on a policy that has not is confounded with incomplete optimization: harder to read as transfer, not uninterpretable. We use two checks. The behavioral check compares held-out and training-level return, under the policy’s own sampled actions, with the random floor; it needs no threshold, normalizer, or action-space assumption. The screen is final-checkpoint policy entropy relative to the maximum-entropy uniform policy ( ln ⁡ 15 = 2.708 \ln 15=2.708 ), in three tiers: converged (entropy < 2.0 <2.0 ), partial ( [ 2.0 , 2.3 ] [2.0,2.3] ), non-converged ( > 2.3 >2.3 ). The screen is cheap and routinely logged; the behavioral check is what a tier should be read against. Entropy alone cannot deliver a verdict: a high-entropy policy may be a legitimately stochastic policy and a legitimate object of evaluation, and a low-entropy policy may still perform poorly. Entropy is the mean over the train- and test-level evaluation passes; at 25M we report heist under both that convention and the test-level value alone, because the two differ enough to change its label (Appendix B ). The entropy bonus is not the only configuration choice that moves the measurement. Retraining heist with c H = 0.001 c_{H}=0.001 instead of the default 0.01 0.01 gives a terminal entropy of 2.113 ± 0.038 2.113\pm 0.038 ( 78.0 % 78.0\% of maximum; n = 3 n{=}3 seeds per encoder, 8M), against 2.565 2.565 ( 94.7 % 94.7\% ) for the default runs. Those retrains, however, used 256 parallel environments rather than the 16 of the default 8M runs (Appendix F ), so the difference cannot be attributed to c H c_{H} ; it shows only that the screen’s value depends on the training configuration, which is one more reason to read it against the behavioral check. The two checks agree at the extremes and disagree in the middle (Table 3 ). Starpilot is converged by entropy and far above the floor; heist is the least converged by entropy and the only environment whose sampled held-out return is at the floor. Between them the screen over-calls. Bossfight is non-converged by entropy yet its sampled policy scores clearly above the floor on held-out levels ( 1.38 1.38 vs. 0.09 0.09 , z ≈ 2.6 z\approx 2.6 ), and dodgeball, also non-converged, is above its floor ( 1.12 1.12 vs. 0.47 0.47 , z ≈ 3.0 z\approx 3.0 ). Part of the over-call is the action space: entropy over ProcGen’s 15 raw actions counts probability spread across actions with identical effects as indecision, and 35–65% of each environment’s raw entropy is of that kind (Appendix D ). Merging equivalent actions before computing entropy leaves one environment short of the converged band (heist) when equivalence is determined state by state, and three (dodgeball, bossfight, heist) under a single partition per game; these counts depend on expressing the 2.0 and 2.3 cuts as fractions of the maximum, which is our choice. We keep raw-action entropy for the tiers because it is what practitioners log, and read a partial or non-converged tier as a prompt to run the behavioral check, not as a finding that the policy has not learned. Two robustness checks address whether the entropy cut point is load-bearing. First, sweeping the converged/partial boundary across [ 1.8 , 2.2 ] [1.8,2.2] leaves the two extreme calls unchanged (starpilot is converged and heist non-converged at every value), while the intermediate environments near 2.0 move with the cut point, which is precisely why they carry the partial label rather than a verdict (Appendix B ). This sweep bounds the borderline calls only: starpilot ( 1.799 1.799 ) and heist ( 2.565 2.565 ) are the extremes of the observed range, so no interior cut point could reclassify them, and their stability under the sweep follows from the data layout rather than from robustness. Second, a diagnostic that never thresholds the final entropy (the total collapse of entropy from its initial plateau, combined with training-set return) ranks environments consistently with the tiers (Spearman ρ = 0.79 \rho=0.79 ; Appendix C ); it shares the terminal-entropy trajectory as an input, so it is a second reading rather than a fully independent one. 3.5 Statistical analysis Encoder and train-vs-test comparisons use Welch’s t t -test. Where we pool across independent draws (seeds), per-draw two-sided p p -values are combined with Fisher’s method, with Stouffer’s Z Z on the one-sided p p -values as a directional cross-check; confidence intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap ( 10 4 10^{4} resamples). Per-environment pooled results, and one instructive case where the omnibus and directional combiners disagree, are in Appendix A . 4 Field-Wide Audit To document how ProcGen generalization numbers are produced in practice, we audited the released evaluation code of twelve prior ProcGen codebases spanning ICML, NeurIPS, RLC, and arXiv from 2019 to 2025. What we looked for. For each repository we located the code path that produces the paper’s reported test numbers. We then classified two binary properties: (i) stochastic evaluation , whether test-time actions are sampled from the policy distribution rather than chosen by greedy argmax; and (ii) in-loop test returns , whether reported test returns are read from a held-out rollout that runs concurrently inside the training loop—stepped alongside training, never reset between updates, and reported as a running mean over the most recent completed episodes, which therefore span several policy versions—rather than from a dedicated evaluation of a fixed checkpoint. Property (ii) is deliberately narrower than it may sound: in every codebase we mark, the held-out environments or workers contribute no gradient, so the test returns are not returns from the rollout the policy is trained on. Classifications were made against a pinned commit, and the evidencing file and line for every entry are listed in Appendix E so the classification is reproducible against the precise code state. For codebases with an explicit evaluation script, the cited line is the test-time action-selection call; for the in-loop codebases, the cited lines are where the held-out environment or worker is created and where its running return is reported. What we found. Eleven of twelve codebases perform held-out evaluation; all eleven evaluate their policy-gradient agents stochastically, and six of those additionally report in-loop test returns (Table 1 ). UCB-DrAC ( Raileanu et al., 2021 ) is the most explicit instance, passing deterministic=False at test.py line 42. Impoola ( Trumpp et al., 2025 ) also sets the rule explicitly, through a documented configuration option: its PPO evaluation samples and its DQN evaluation is greedy, as its paper states. EDE ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) is itself a value-based method: its released code samples when evaluating its PPO baseline, which is the row we classify, while EDE’s own agent is evaluated ϵ \epsilon -greedily with ϵ = 0.05 \epsilon=0.05 , the standard DQN evaluation protocol. For a value-based agent the greedy action is the trained policy, so neither case bears on the sampled-versus-argmax analysis of Section 5.1 , which concerns stochastic policies. VSOP and VSOP-3D ( Jesson et al., 2024 ; Jesson and Jiang, 2024 ) step a separate held-out environment once per training step and report the mean of its last 100 episodes. A classification we checked and rejected. These six codebases are easily read as rollout-mode —reading test returns off the on-policy training rollout, a train-vs-test procedure mismatch—and our own first pass classified them that way. Checking each against its pinned commit shows that classification is wrong. In mixreg, the ProcGen baseline, and IBAC-SNI the test numbers come from a dedicated MPI test worker whose gradient is weighted to zero; in RAD, VSOP, and VSOP-3D they come from a separate held-out environment whose transitions are discarded. In all six the train number comes from the matching in-loop procedure on the training levels, so train and test are measured the same way. What remains is the weaker property defined above: the test number is a sampled-action running average taken during training, not a measurement of the final policy. Our cited location for mixreg was also wrong: it pointed at an evaluation runner the training script never enables. The twelfth, PPG ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , trains on the full level distribution and performs no held-out evaluation in its released code, so neither classification applies (n/a). Provenance. Nine of the eleven set no rule at the point of evaluation. Three (DAAC, PLR, and EDE’s PPO baseline) inherit sampling through a default argument that no call site overrides, and the six in-loop codebases sample through the training rollout’s own sampling call, which has no deterministic path. In these nine, nothing in the evaluation code selects the rule or states a reason for it. That is how the practice became field-wide: an evaluation default propagated through copied harness code. The two exceptions show that the rule can be set deliberately: UCB-DrAC passes deterministic=False at the call site, and Impoola exposes the rule as a configuration option, sampling for PPO and acting greedily for DQN. By the analysis of Section 5.1 , the default happens to be the better of the two rules for policies that have not converged; the concern is that where it is inherited, its consequences for the reported gap go unexamined. Scope of the claim. We audited released evaluation code, not results as reported in papers, and we do not claim any specific published number is wrong. The claim is about what the procedure can support. A gap whose train and test numbers come from different procedures cannot distinguish a protocol difference from a distributional one; we found no such case in the audit, but the hazard is general. An in-loop gap is matched, but it averages over the policies visited during training rather than measuring any one of them.
